paper_title: Work2Skill: Capturing Human GUI Experience for Reusable Agent Skill Induction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex GUI tasks, yet unfamiliar software and workflows requiring human domain knowledge remain challenging. Human demonstrations convey procedural knowledge through the same GUI interaction space, but reuse requires interpreting actions in context and separating workflow rules from task-specific details. We thus introduce Work2Skill, a framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction. WorkRecorder provides the framework's infrastructure for collecting this experience, aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available accessibility-tree information. Using WorkRecorder, we construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. Its 350 demonstrations are screened for completeness and task success. We then propose an agentic skill-induction method that inspects evidence on demand to produce reusable skills capturing workflow rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. When the same four execution models are equipped with skills induced by each method under shared execution settings, Work2Skill achieves the highest scores and success rates. Mean score improvements over the corresponding No Skill baseline are 4.67--10.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.11--7.50 points on a 286-task subset of OSWorld-Verified. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/china-qijizhifeng/Work2Skill.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Computer-use agents can perform increasingly complex desktop and web tasks, supported by advances in GUI grounding and planning (Qin et al., 2025; Agashe et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a). Yet agents still struggle with unfamiliar software and workflows that require domain knowledge, where successful execution depends on procedures not spelled out in the users request (Zhang et al., 2026e; Jang et al., 2026). For example, submit my reimbursement does not specify which internal portal to use, which receipts to attach, or what to check before submission. Agents need this useror organization-specific procedural knowledge to translate users goal into GUI actions. Human demonstrations offer direct source of this knowledge because humans and computer-use agents share the same GUI interaction space. Demonstrated controls, action sequences, and visible outcomes can therefore guide an agents own execution. Prior work converts demonstrations into expert instructions and semantic action traces (Li et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026e), multimodal tutorials (Bai et al., 2026), or reusable skills 1 Figure 1: Work2Skill framework: WorkRecorder, WorkDemo-350, and Agentic Skill Induction.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: (Yang et al., 2026a; Xiao et al., 2026). OpenAIs Record & Replay (OpenAI, 2026b) and Claudes Record skill (Anthropic, 2026b) bring this approach to user-facing tools. We thus introduce Work2Skill, framework that captures human GUI experience for reusable agent skill induction (Figure 1). Its three components address the following challenges in action grounding, method comparison, and evidence inspection. First, action coordinates reveal where an operation occurred but not what the target control means. ShowUI-Aloha interprets actions from full-screen frames and target crops (Zhang et al., 2026e), while Demo2Tutorial uses before-and-after screenshots (Bai et al., 2026). Without accessibilitytree (AX) evidence, these parsers depend on visual grounding to infer target semantics; selected frames can also miss transient states and intermediate operations. WorkRecorder addresses this ambiguity by aligning screen recordings, mouse and keyboard events, and available AX information. Recorded element names and roles provide explicit control semantics, while linked video preserves the surrounding state changes. The induction agent can thus interpret an operation using both its visual context and available structured UI evidence. Second, representative desktop GUI studies use different demonstrations, task sets, and execution protocols (Zhang et al., 2026e; Bai et al., 2026). Their results mix differences in induction with differences in source experience and evaluation conditions. WorkDemo-350 provides common demonstration resource for skill induction in desktop environments. Collected with WorkRecorder, it contains 350 human GUI demonstrations covering 64 MyPCBench Bounded Action tasks (Jang et al., 2026) and 286-task OSWorld-Verified subset (Xie et al., 2024). Each demonstration is screened for completeness and task success and packaged with synchronized visual and action evidence, plus available AX information. This shared evidence and controlled downstream protocol support comparisons of induction methods using the same task evaluators and execution conditions. Third, representative pipelines prescribe an order for action parsing and procedure abstraction, even when individual stages refine their outputs (Zhang et al., 2026e; Bai et al., 2026). This couples evidence inspection to predefined stages. Loading long recording into context at once also creates context pressure, while selecting fixed subset can omit details needed later. Our agentic skillinduction method addresses both constraints by interleaving on-demand evidence inspection with skill writing and revision. Drawing on active evidence acquisition in agentic video understanding (Yuan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), the agent selects linked files, images, and video intervals to resolve questions as they arise. It can revisit the source after drafting without loading the entire recording at once. During skill writing, we guide the agent to generalize demonstration-specific inputs into task-dependent descriptions while preserving procedural rules, step dependencies, and completion checks. The skills guide execution without the source recording. We evaluate the resulting skills through downstream execution on the WorkDemo-350 tasks. Using official evaluators and shared text-guidance interface, we compare Work2Skill with No Skill and text-adapted versions of ShowUI-Aloha and Demo2Tutorial. Across four execution models, Work2Skill improves mean evaluation scores over No Skill by 4.6710.54 points on MyPCBench Bounded Action and 3.117.50 points on the evaluated OSWorld-Verified subset. Further experiments test reuse under changed requirements within the same application (MyPCBench Jitter) and transfer between two execution models. Evidence ablations and the Pipeline Prompt comparison examine the roles of input modalities and induction-prompt design. Our contributions are threefold: 1) We introduce WorkRecorder, the human GUI experience collection infrastructure of Work2Skill, which aligns recorded inputs with visual and available AX evidence to clarify demonstrated actions. 2) We construct WorkDemo-350, the first synchronized multimodal dataset of human desktop GUI demonstrations for reusable agent skill induction and downstream evaluation. 3) We propose an agentic skill induction method that interleaves on-demand evidence inspection with skill writing and revision. Across two benchmarks and four execution models, it achieves the highest scores and success rates among the evaluated methods.

They support data collection, grounding, model training (Wang et al., 2025a; Nayak et al., 2025; Feizi et al., 2026) and agent efficiency evaluation (Abhyankar et al., 2026). Demonstration structure can also influence task execution (Xing et al., 2026). Procedural representations include expert instructions (Li et al., 2025), task graphs (Yin et al., 2025), and parameterized workflows for robust replay (Zhao et al., 2026). LearnAct also introduces LearnGUI for evaluating demonstration-based learning on mobile devices (Liu et al., 2026). More recent work includes semantic action traces, multimodal tutorials, natural-language skill graphs, and standard operating procedure (SOP) skills (Zhang et al., 2026e; Bai et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a; Xiao et al., 2026). Skill Induction and Active Evidence Acquisition. Reusable guidance draws on experience organization and evidence selection. Skill-induction methods learn procedures through autonomous interaction (Wang et al., 2025b; Zheng et al., 2025) or distill execution and user traces (Mi et al., 2026; Ni et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026c), with environment feedback and policy learning supporting further refinement (Xia et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b). Adaptive memories, contextual playbooks, and learned memory-management routines retain experience (Suzgun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c;a), while experience-based evaluation examines its downstream value (Peng et al., 2026). Guidance from multimodal demonstrations requires choosing what to inspect. Agentic video methods retrieve and examine relevant segments iteratively (Ma et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). In GUI settings, CUADebug inspects traces and screenshots to diagnose execution failures (Zhang et al., 2026d), while MMSkills packages textual procedures, state cards, and keyframes for selective inspection during execution (Zhang et al., 2026b).

sections.title: 3 WORK2SKILL FRAMEWORK
sections.content: Work2Skill connects human demonstrations to reusable procedural guidance (Figure 2). WorkRecorder preserves actions together with their visual and semantic context; WorkDemo-350 organizes the collected demonstrations into curated evidence resource. An induction agent inspects this evidence, revisits unclear steps, and writes skills for downstream GUI execution.

sections.title: 3.1 WORKRECORDER
sections.content: WorkRecorder collects the evidence needed to interpret human actions in context. Given task instruction, human demonstrator performs the task in the benchmarks official environment.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Figure 3: Human GUI experience collection with WorkRecorder. demonstrated workflow (left) is captured and reviewed through the recorder interface (center), then organized into an evidence episode with task metadata, action traces, and available multimodal evidence (right). WorkRecorder captures screen video, keyframe images, mouse and keyboard activity, and available UI information as multimodal evidence (Figure 3). An action trace links each recorded operation to its supporting evidence so that the induction agent can inspect individual steps. Task setup and outcome evaluation follow the corresponding benchmark procedures. macOS interface records local workflows or interactions with remote Linux desktop. For remote tasks, the Mac captures the displayed workflow and local inputs, while collector in the target environment supplies UI evidence. Platform-specific collectors provide target-element metadata, accessibility-tree (AX) snapshots, and application or window context when available. Coverage depends on the recording configuration and the applications accessibility support. Multimodal Capture and Alignment. WorkRecorder aligns input events and visual observations on common video-relative timeline. It groups timestamped events into actions such as clicks, drags, scrolling, and hotkeys, then links these actions to keyframes. An agent can therefore inspect click alongside its screen image, available target information, and surrounding video to determine what changed. Target-element association uses pointer location and event timing, with window context and control semantics helping select among candidates. On Linux, AT-SPI point queries and nearby accessibility events supply available names, roles, and bounds for click and drag records. UI annotations are derived from the corresponding target elements in the AX tree. AX snapshots provide additional interface context but need not reflect the exact action-time state. Appendix details the recording architecture, capture policies, target-matching rules, and time alignment. Evidence Representation and Packaging. Each demonstration becomes an evidence episode containing the task instruction and metadata, an ordered action trace, and the available multimodal evidence. manifest indexes these resources; action records link to keyframes and video times. These links support targeted inspection without processing the recording sequentially. Descriptions help locate operations; linked recordings let the agent verify their interpretation. The available evidence depends on capture and export settings. Appendix provides details.

sections.title: 3.3 AGENTIC SKILL INDUCTION
sections.content: Skill induction turns an evidence episode into reusable procedural guidance. Given the task instruction and recorded evidence, NexAU tool-using agent (Nex-AGI, 2026) generates skills in an output directory separate from the recordings. The default system prompt is concise: it sets evidence-access boundaries, prerequisite checks, and completion requirements while leaving the detailed exploration and revision sequence to the agent. bundled skill-creator policy guides skill authoring. After reading this policy and the task definition in task.json, the agent alternates evidence inspection with skill writing and revision. Appendix provides the prompts and authoring policy. Evidence Exploration Tools. We select file, image, and video tools that expose complementary views of demonstration at different granularities. File discovery and reading provide task definitions, manifests, action traces, key logs, and available structured UI evidence. Traces and indices link operations to their supporting media, while AX records supply available control names and roles. read visual evidence returns selected images with source-path labels, exposing visible controls and entered or selected values. Video tools provide access to states and transitions beyond the indexed images. After reading video metadata, the agent can sample an interval with watch video or request individual timestamps with extract video frames; both return timestamp-labeled frames. Source-path and timestamp labels preserve the correspondence between returned observations and source artifacts. Appendix details the interfaces, and Section 4.5 evaluates the contribution of the available evidence to downstream execution. Active Evidence Acquisition. The agent chooses its next observation according to the task and unresolved questions in the evidence, following iterative inspection in agentic video understanding (Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). The prompt requires representative initial, critical, and final-state images to be inspected when indexed images are available; the agent otherwise determines the inspection sequence and level of detail. For example, an ambiguous click can prompt inspection of the target frame to identify the control, followed by later video frame to check the resulting state. Tool guidance encourages coarse video sampling followed by closer examination of relevant actions. Evidence inspection and skill writing share one conversation, so draft can expose missing constraints or unverified transitions. The agent can then return to the relevant evidence and revise the procedure to incorporate supported dependencies and completion checks. Candidate skills are not executed during induction, and downstream evaluation results are not used as revision feedback. When the available observations do not resolve an uncertainty, the authoring policy requires an observable conditional check or an explicit limitation in the skill. Section 4.5 compares this prompt with Pipeline Prompt, which sets exploration order but allows further inspection.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Skill Generation. The agent expresses each coherent reusable capability in SKILL.md, with YAML frontmatter containing its name and description, following the Agent Skills file convention (Zhang et al., 2025). Through the authoring policy, we guide the agent to generalize demonstrationspecific inputs into task-dependent descriptions and describe UI targets semantically. The policy instructs the agent to keep phases together when they share state, task-derived data, quantities, or required ordering, and to retain selection rules, calculations, dependencies, requested scope, stop conditions, visible completion checks, and supported recovery. Skills must preserve visible GUI interaction and include all instructions needed for execution without the source recording. Before completion, the agent calls finalize extraction to validate output structure and required tool use. Checks cover task-file access, required skill structure, recorded write followed by read of each final skill, and metadata inspection before video sampling. Successful finalization records skill hashes, inspected source paths, validation results, and run provenance. These checks verify output structure and required tool use; they do not verify skill correctness or task success. For downstream evaluation, the executor receives the target task instruction and generated skill. It selects GUI actions using this guidance together with its observations and action history, without accessing the source recording. Sections 4.4 and 4.3 evaluate reuse across execution models and task instances. Appendix D.4 details the authoring policy and output requirements.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We organize our experiments around the following four research questions. RQ1 tests whether the induced skills improve execution on the demonstrated tasks. RQ2 and RQ3 then examine two dimensions of reuse: changes to task requirements and changes to the execution model, respectively. RQ4 investigates how the available evidence and induction prompt affect downstream utility. case study illustrates how induced skills handle dependent subgoals in multistep workflow.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate on the 64 MyPCBench Bounded Action tasks and 286 OSWorldVerified tasks in WorkDemo-350 using official task evaluators. On MyPCBench, the execution agent has access to both GUI actions and Bash commands. Benchmark selection and demonstration screening are described in Section 3.2. OSWorld results apply to this curated subset. Appendix E.3 describes our OSWorld execution harness and evaluator configuration. Skill-based Evaluation. We evaluate skills as plug-in guidance by appending their text as clearly delimited block to the end of the executors base system prompt. All text-guidance methods use the same <task skills> wrapper; Appendix D.5 gives the template and injected contents. Separating procedural guidance from the execution loop supports reuse across execution models and integration with different agent harnesses. We therefore use shared execution settings for each model and benchmark, varying only the appended guidance to control for differences in native agent pipelines. We compare Work2Skill with No Skill, action semantics from ShowUI-Aloha (Aloha) (Zhang et al., 2026e), and tutorial text from Demo2Tutorial (D2T) (Bai et al., 2026). The demonstration-based methods use the same source episodes, while their input modalities and evidence representations follow each methods design. RQ1 thus compares their overall ability to produce useful guidance under shared execution conditions; RQ4 separately examines evidence and induction-prompt choices within Work2Skill while holding the model and skill-authoring policy fixed. Models and Metrics. We use GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026a), Opus-4.8 (Anthropic, 2026a), Qwen3.535B-A3B, and Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026). By default, the same model induces skills and executes tasks with them; RQ3 varies this pairing. We report mean evaluation score (Score, 0 100), full-credit success rate (SR), mean execution steps, and mean skill-induction token usage. Appendix details task selection, metrics, baseline adaptations, and execution settings.

sections.title: 4.4 RQ3: DO SKILLS TRANSFER ACROSS MODELS?
sections.content: To evaluate whether induced skills transfer across models, we separate induction from execution and test guidance produced by one model with different executor. We cross GPT-5.5 and Qwen3.5-9B as induction and execution models, freezing each induced skill before downstream evaluation (Figure 4). Skills induced by GPT-5.5 outperform those induced by Qwen3.5-9B under both executors. The advantage is larger with GPT-5.5 execution, reaching 9.46 score points and 9.38 percentage points in success rate, but remains positive after transfer to Qwen3.5-9B. All four pairings improve on the No Skill baseline for the same executor. Performance remains substantially lower with Qwen3.5-9B execution regardless of the induction model. Thus, the skills transfer usefully between these two models, but stronger induction does not close the performance gap between executors on these tasks. sections.title: 4.5 RQ4: HOW DO EVIDENCE AND INDUCTION PROMPTS AFFECT SKILL INDUCTION?
sections.content: To assess how evidence and prompts affect downstream skill utility, we ablate the available input modalities and separately compare the Work2Skill and Pipeline Prompt system prompts. For the evidence ablation, we vary induction evidence on 64 MyPCBench tasks with GPT-5.5, keeping reasoning effort (high) and the iteration limit fixed. UI annotations contain metadata and descriptions derived from the corresponding action targets in the AX tree. The w/o KeyLogs condition removes both raw logs and added image overlays while retaining the action trace and its UI target information. Appendix E.6 details the inputs and prompt adaptations. Full Evidence scores 85.27 and fully solves 31 tasks (Figure 5a). Removing indexed images, UI annotations, or KeyLogs reduces Score by 5.0210.63 points and SR by 14.0621.88 percentage points. The largest drops are in Score without indexed images and SR without KeyLogs. UI-Grounded Action Text Only uses ordered action descriptions with target UI semantics. It outperforms Video-only and uses the fewest steps; both trail Full Evidence in Score and SR. Fewer steps do not necessarily indicate better task completion; Score and SR remain essential for interpreting execution efficiency.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: With the evidence held fixed, we next test whether prescribed sequence of induction stages helps the agent use it. Our concise default prompt leaves detailed evidence exploration and skill revision to the agent. Pipeline Prompt specifies the induction stages and their order: read the task and artifacts, inspect images and video, then write, review, and finalize skills. Only the system prompt changes; the model, evidence, tools, authoring policy, and output format remain fixed (Appendix D.3). Both prompts allow further evidence inspection. In Figure 5b, Work2Skill improves Score by 3.97 points and SR by 6.25 percentage points, while reducing average execution steps from 48.98 to 47.38, at 12.7% higher skill-induction token usage. In this setting, Full Evidence yields the best Score and SR among the tested input configurations, while the Work2Skill prompt outperforms the prescribed pipeline at higher induction cost. Together, these comparisons show how evidence and prompt design affect the downstream utility of generated skills. sections.title: 4.6 CASE STUDY
sections.content: To illustrate how extracted skill guidance affects execution, we compare GPT-5.5 supplied with outputs from ShowUI-Aloha, D2T, or Work2Skill through the shared text interface (Section 4.1). Each method extracts its guidance from the same human demonstration. Figure 6 shows Cotogna booking for ten people with three fallback restaurants and two favorites. The fallbacks must be handled before confirmation, while preserving the date, party size, and requested note. With ShowUI-Aloha or D2T guidance, the executor completes the primary booking but leaves fallback inspection, favoriting, and persistence checks incomplete, scoring 55/100 in both conditions. With the skill induced by Work2Skill, it satisfies all eight rubric items (100/100). The generated skill makes intermediate requirements explicit: it rechecks fields that may reset during navigation, excludes the primary restaurant from the fallback set, and defers final confirmation until the fallback steps are complete. The skill preserves dependent subgoals across navigation and checks both the reservation and saved favorites before declaring completion (Appendix F.2).

sections.content: We presented Work2Skill, framework for capturing human GUI experience and converting it into reusable agent skills. WorkRecorder collects aligned multimodal evidence, WorkDemo-350 organizes 350 curated demonstrations, and agentic skill induction combines on-demand evidence inspection with iterative skill writing and revision. sections.title: A RECORDER IMPLEMENTATION
sections.content: A.1 ARCHITECTURE AND DEPLOYMENT WorkRecorder consists of native macOS recording application, local service for capture coordination and storage, and accessibility providers. In local macOS mode, the application records the selected screen region and input activity, with available accessibility evidence supplied by the macOS provider. For remote Linux workflow, recording remains on the Mac, while an AT-SPI collector runs inside the target desktop session. The Linux launcher connects this collector to the local service through an SSH tunnel; the remote-desktop client supplies the displayed workflow. Task initialization and official benchmark evaluation are handled separately from recording. Video and input capture. The macOS application records selected screen region through ScreenCaptureKit and encodes video with H.264. CoreGraphics event taps supply mouse and keyboard activity, which is also grouped into semantic operations. The operator can pause, resume, stop, and review recording. Full keystroke capture is disabled by default; when enabled, it records key presses and releases, characters, modifiers, and timestamps. Otherwise, ordinary typing is represented through aggregate typing events. The capture policy therefore determines the detail available in the input stream. Accessibility evidence. The Linux collector supports X11/Xorg desktops and uses AT-SPI to obtain Accessibility Trees, interface events, and target UI elements. Its default periodic tree sampler runs every two seconds, with limits of six levels and 400 nodes; these are implementation defaults rather than dataset collection settings. Events may reference the latest completed tree snapshot, with its sampling timestamps. Target-element queries return available names, roles, and bounds at screen location. The recorder maps positions in the displayed remote-desktop region to Linux desktop coordinates for these queries. Availability depends on application accessibility support and sampling limits. Target-element association. When resolving clicks from accessibility snapshots, the resolver considers nodes whose bounds contain the click coordinate. It ranks these candidates by node confidence and interactive role, with an area penalty favoring smaller controls. Resolution records retain the selected source, confidence, and evidence anchor; uncertain cases can remain flagged for review. The remote Linux probing path is triggered by clicks and drags. Configured remote-display geometry maps local pointer positions to Linux desktop pixels; positions outside the displayed desktop do not trigger point probe. The AT-SPI watcher combines bounded point queries with nearby focus, selection, and state-change events. Its point-query ranking prioritizes active windows, named interactive controls, other named nodes, greater depth, and smaller area, in that order. Event correlation normally checks whether the target bounds contain the pointer position, with additional handling for transient controls such as menus that disappear after selection. Pointer-resolution records retain the originating pointer sequence identifier and distinguish resolved, coarse, unresolved, and error or timeout outcomes. During export, recorded probe results are associated with actions using their triggers monotonic In normal export timestamp and action kind, with nearest-action fallback within 2.5 seconds. mode, missing click or drag target can also be recovered from the nearest specific accessibility event within 3-second window. This backfill excludes generic page or window focus and uses each candidate event at most once. For drags, the matching anchor is the drag start, computed from the release time and recorded duration. Backfilled records retain their source, event identifier, and time offset. These are heuristic temporal associations; the matching windows are implementation tolerances, not measured accuracy bounds. Keyboard input does not trigger this Linux target probe. AX snapshots are attached independently as interface context. A.2 KEYFRAME SELECTION Capture triggers. WorkRecorder selects keyframes primarily around recorded operations and interface transitions. Recording start, stop, pause, and resume provide boundary frames, while users can explicitly mark additional frames. Routine candidates are triggered by clicks, drag releases,

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: scroll completion, recognized hotkeys, command submission, and window or tab switches. typing pause can trigger frame when text is submitted or typing milestone is reached; the default milestone requires at least eight characters or input events in the typing segment. Individual key presses and releases do not independently trigger screenshots. Additional enabled policies can request frames at scroll milestones or when provider reports an error or warning surface. Action context and capture timing. For clicks, hotkeys, and window or tab switches, the recorder can reuse recent preceding keyframe as before-action context, with default freshness limit of 1.5 seconds. new before-action capture requires an explicit pre-action event; otherwise this context can remain unavailable. Result frames use bounded settling window to allow the interface to respond. With adaptive polling enabled, capture can proceed when provider reports readiness or when visual or text observations stabilize after detected change; the default stability rule requires two consecutive stable samples. Waiting limits depend on the action type. If settling times out, the policy can capture the available state and flag it for review, or suppress the candidate. Thus, result-frame link does not by itself establish that the interface has finished updating. Candidate filtering. The planner removes duplicate triggers within an actions timing plan. The scheduler applies minimum gap between separate plans, limits result frames per action, and enforces capture budgets. When change or quality signals are available, it can also reject candidates with insufficient change or information gain. Defaults include 500-ms gap, at most two resultrelated candidates per action, and session budget of 64 keyframes; required boundary frames and explicit user marks have exemptions. These are implementation defaults, not verified settings for every collected demonstration. Retained keyframes carry identifiers and timestamps, while trigger decisions retain acceptance or rejection reasons. Frame reuse and candidate filtering mean that actions and keyframes need not have one-to-one correspondence. Exported image counts are distinguished from recorded keyframe counts in Appendix B. A.3 TIME ALIGNMENT The recorder maps evidence onto the stitched videos timeline. Native input uses monotonic timestamp anchored to the first captured frame of each recording segment, rather than the time at which recording was requested. Remote Linux events use wall-clock timestamps, which are projected onto the same timeline using the corresponding first-frame wall-clock anchors and segment durations. Segment offsets account for pause/resume boundaries; remote events falling within pause have no corresponding video frame. The Linux launcher checks host clock agreement before recording and rejects difference greater than two seconds. This check is deployment condition, not measured alignment-error bound. Legacy recordings without first-frame wall-clock anchors use the session start as fallback.

sections.title: B EVIDENCE SCHEMA
sections.content: B.1 EPISODE FILES FOR SKILL INDUCTION The induction agent reads per-task episode directory containing the task and its recorded evidence. The benchmark converter creates three core files: task.json, episode.json, and trace/actions.jsonl. Input logs, video, summaries, and images are included when available  (Table 4)  . The task file must contain the authoritative instruction and task inputs; placeholder with only an inferred task ID is insufficient for induction. The converter excludes the grading field from this file. The episode.json manifest identifies the task and recording, records duration and evidence counts, and indexes the available files. Evidence paths are relative to the episode directory. Its source entry records the original export location for provenance; that location is not an additional input root for the agent.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Table 4: Files exposed to the induction agent in converted episode. The first three files form the core structure; the remaining artifacts are included when available. File or directory task.json episode.json trace/actions.jsonl trace/keylog.jsonl video.mp4 summary.md evidence/ Content Task instruction and associated task metadata. File references, recording metadata, and counts. Normalized action records in temporal order. Recorded input-event log. Recording video. Textual operation summary. Evidence images, with available image manifests and actionassociation indices. B.2 ACTION RECORDS AND IMAGE ASSOCIATIONS Each line of trace/actions.jsonl describes recorded action, with its identifier, sequence index, action kind, video-relative timestamp, and caption. Coordinates and target information are retained when available. The following excerpt reproduces selected fields from the first action in the hard app-f016 episode used in Appendix F: { } "sequence_index": 0, "action_id": "act_0JYEZK480Ta_81AR", "kind": "click", "media_time_ms": 3908, "caption": "Left Click push button - Calendar", "target_label": "push button - Calendar" When present, evidence/manifest.json and evidence/image actions.jsonl provide the image index and its input-event and trajectory associations. In this episode, the first image-index record references the same action id, with frame time ms = 3908 and action delta ms = 0. These fields let the agent locate the corresponding event frame and nearby video observations. nonzero action delta ms indicates an approximate temporal match. An event frame captures the interface near the input event; verifying its effect may require subsequent observation. B.3 EVIDENCE AVAILABILITY AND COUNTS The schema describes the files available within an episode, rather than guaranteeing every modality for every demonstration. Target metadata in an action record does not imply that complete accessibility-tree sequence is included. In Linux mode, the continuous tree sequence remains in the Linux evidence directory, while the Mac export can preserve snapshots received with events. The induction agent can inspect only the evidence provided within its exposed input directory. The manifest distinguishes action records, input events, recorded keyframes, and exported evidence images. Table 1 reports mean counts of action records and exported images per episode. The hard app-f016 episode, for example, contains 37 action records and 23 evidence images, alongside 176 input events and 29 recorded keyframes. Action and image counts differ because they use separate grouping rules. Image export pairs key presses with releases, groups double clicks, and merges adjacent typing evidence into one image with the last frame and combined text annotation. Scroll records do not independently generate images, while action preprocessing merges adjacent typing and scroll records. The converter sets counts.keyframes from the recordings keyframe count, falling back to the number of loaded keyframe records; counts.evidence images counts images copied into the main evidence collection. Exporting all available keyframe screenshots is separate option that creates evidence/all keyframes/ and its own manifest. Recorded keyframes thus reflect the capture policies in Appendix A.2; exported images reflect subsequent evidence processing.

Task interpretation, action selection, and comparisons between observations are performed by the agent using the returned evidence. The following descriptions summarize the registered tools and their principal arguments. File discovery and reading. list directory takes dir path; glob takes pattern and optional dir path. Both support filtering options. read file takes file path, with optional zerobased line offset and limit. It handles text, JSON, JSONL, YAML, and Markdown as text, returns numbered lines and continuation guidance, and directs image and video requests to the corresponding visual tools. response is limited to 20,000 characters of numbered content; individual long lines are truncated. This interface provides access to task metadata, action traces, input logs, image indices, and any exported structured UI artifacts. Image inspection. read visual evidence takes an ordered file paths list containing 120 distinct images. Optional image detail and image max size control detail and resizing. Returned images preserve the requested order and have source-path labels, allowing the agent to compare selected states while retaining their file identities. sections.title: F CASE STUDY AND SKILL INDUCTION EXAMPLE
sections.content: F.1 TASK AND INDUCTION TRACE We present the generated skill for MyPCBench Bounded Action task hard app-f016, TableFind reservation task also used in the main-text case study (Section 4.6). The task instruction is: Book me Cotogna for ten people for the Dundies after-party next Friday. While youre in TableFind, pull up three other Scranton-area restaurants as fallback plan in case Cotogna is full, and favorite the top two. Once thats done, confirm the Cotogna reservation with note that its the Dundies after-party so they can prep the vibe. The recorded induction run uses GPT-5.5 with high reasoning effort and makes 30 tool calls. It reads the task, episode metadata, summary, evidence indices, action trace, and key log; inspects 22 distinct evidence images in two batches of 14 and eight; and samples the 156.47-second video in two calls to watch video, after reading its metadata. The video calls return 13 and eight frames, respectively, with one shared timestamp. The agent writes draft, reads it back, revises it, and reads the final skill before successful finalize extraction. This record documents the induction output; we do not assign downstream execution score to this listing. F.2 DETAILED EXECUTION ANALYSIS Figure 6 shows GPT-5.5s execution trajectories for the case in Section 4.6. Table 11 reports all eight rubric outcomes under ShowUI-Aloha, D2T, and Work2Skill guidance. Task dependencies. The instruction combines primary reservation with fallback workflow: inspect three other Scranton-area restaurants and favorite the top two before confirming Cotogna with the requested note. Completing this workflow requires carrying the date and party size across searches, distinguishing the primary restaurant from alternatives, and returning to the primary booking after handling the fallbacks. The evaluation checks both the reservation itself and these additional requirements, including persistence after refresh. Where the baselines fall short. Both baselines pass R1, R2, R6, and R8: they configure the booking, include the note, obtain confirmation, and verify the final reservation details. Their trajectories reach alternative-restaurant views, but the rubric outcomes do not establish that all three alternatives and their detail pages were inspected (R3R4). Saving the top two alternatives is also incomplete (R5). Both fail the separate persistence check (R7), despite passing the check of final details (R8). visible confirmation and correct reservation display therefore cover only part of the required workflow. Each baseline receives 55/100.

Restaurant names and booking values are taken from the task, while the generated procedure retains the Scranton-area scope. Its final checks use visible reservation and favorite states.

sections.content: Figure 9 summarizes tool usage during skill induction by four models on 64 MyPCBench Bounded Action tasks and the 286-task OSWorld-Verified subset. Each value is the aggregate invocation count divided by the datasets task count; the summary row includes all ten tools. Figure 9: Mean tool calls per task during skill induction, using shared linear color scale. Values are rounded to two decimals; positive values that would round to zero are shown as < 0.01. Horizontal rules separate tool groups; the bold row reports mean total calls per task. Qwen-9B and Qwen-35B denote Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, respectively. GPT-5.5 invokes watch video and extract video frames most frequently on both datasets, while Qwen3.5-35B-A3B makes the fewest total calls per task (14.33 and 12.94). Invocation counts alone do not establish evidence coverage or skill quality: call can return multiple images or varying amounts of text. Repeated finalize extraction calls also do not by themselves identify failed induction runs. When validation fails, the tool returns diagnostics so the agent can address the reported issues and retry. The run can still complete successfully after these intermediate attempts.
